authoritativeText.text:
82. Connecting capacitors — types of capacitor

Electric charge is a property of matter associated with electric pushes and pulls.
Its types are called positive and negative.

Opposite charge amounts can balance in a total without disappearing from the separate places where they are held.
An electric force is such a push or pull, and an electric field describes the electric force per charge at each place.

A capacitor has conducting surfaces, called plates, separated by insulating material.
A conductor lets charge move readily;
an insulator resists this movement.

A capacitor can store separated positive and negative charge, with energy in the electric field between its plates.
Energy is the capacity to produce changes, such as moving an object.

The potential difference, also called voltage, between its plates measures energy transferred per amount of charge moved between them.
A usual overall neutral capacitor has equal charge amounts with opposite signs on its plates.

They balance overall while remaining separated.
Capacitance is the charge magnitude on a single plate per voltage difference, not the net charge of both plates together.

At the same voltage, a capacitor with twice the capacitance stores twice the charge amount on each plate.
An equivalent capacitance is the capacitance of a single capacitor that would give the same charge-voltage relation as a connected group.

Connecting several capacitors can give different equivalent capacitances.
Here we use ideal, linear capacitors: multiplying the voltage by a factor multiplies the stored charge by that factor.

We ignore leakage, unwanted charge escaping through insulation, and stray capacitance, extra capacitance associated with the connecting wires.
Each capacitance is positive.
Parallel and series are the basic connection types.

**Parallel capacitors**
Choose a common reference for electric potential, like choosing a reference level for height.

A point's potential describes electric energy per charge relative to that reference.
A voltage is the difference between potentials at two points.

A **node** is a set of connected conducting points treated as having the same potential.
These points therefore have no voltage difference between them.

In Figure 153, a plate of each capacitor connects to the same node, and its other plate connects to the other node.
Each capacitor therefore has the same voltage across it.

In the charged state shown, the positive plates are connected together, as are the negative plates.
Identify a parallel connection by its nodes, not merely by the signs of the charges currently on the plates.

In this diagram, q labels name plate charges;
a small lower number distinguishes the capacitor.

Vertical bars around a charge symbol mean its magnitude, the amount without its sign.
An outside plus or minus sign shows the positive or negative charge type.

Figure 153

With parallel capacitors at the same voltage, add the charges on the plates connected to a given node.
The equivalent capacitance is therefore the sum of the individual capacitances①.

In the formula, C denotes equivalent capacitance, and C with a small lower number gives that individual capacitor's capacitance.
The lower number is a label, not multiplication.

An equality sign says the expressions on its sides describe the same value.
Plus signs mean add the capacitances;
the continuation dots mean include any further capacitors in the same way:

① Use the definition of capacitance and the relation between charge and voltage to prove equation (8-40) and the following equation (8-41).
For the series proof, the intermediate groups of conductors must initially have zero total charge, with no charge leaking out.

$C=C_1+C_2+C_3+\cdots.$
(8-40)

When at least two positive capacitances are connected in parallel, their equivalent capacitance exceeds any individual capacitance.

**Series capacitors**
In Figure 154, the capacitors connect in sequence.
The conductors between successive capacitors do not connect to other circuit nodes.

Each intermediate conductor group is initially **electrically neutral**, meaning its positive and negative charges balance to give zero total charge.
If no charge leaks out, neighboring plates acquire equal charge amounts with opposite signs through electric induction, the rearrangement of charge under electric forces.

The absolute values of the plate charges are then the same for all the capacitors.
An **absolute value** is the amount without its positive or negative sign.

In the state shown, the first capacitor's negative plate connects to the second capacitor's positive plate, and the later capacitors connect in the same way.
The voltage across the whole group equals the sum of the individual capacitor voltages.

The U labels in this diagram mark the potentials of the left, middle, and right conductor groups relative to the same reference.
They are not three different capacitor voltage drops.

The voltage across each capacitor is the difference between the potentials of its neighboring nodes.
The q annotations show charges, with bars for magnitudes and outside signs for charge type.

Figure 154

Under these ideal series conditions, the reciprocal of the equivalent capacitance equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual capacitances.
A **reciprocal** means one divided by a quantity:
A fraction bar means divide the quantity above it by the quantity below it.

Read the following formula as: one divided by the group capacitance equals the sum of one divided by each individual capacitance.
For two equal capacitors, the same stored charge requires the same voltage on each.
The group needs twice that voltage for the same charge amount, so its equivalent capacitance is half an individual capacitance.

$\frac{1}{C}=\frac{1}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2}+\frac{1}{C_3}+\cdots.$
(8-41)

When at least two positive capacitances are connected in series, the equivalent capacitance is smaller than any individual capacitance.
When choosing real capacitors, also check their permitted operating voltage.

A series connection does not guarantee that the voltage is shared equally.
For the same plate-charge magnitude, a smaller capacitance requires a larger voltage.
Series capacitors share the charge magnitude, so differing capacitances generally receive differing voltages.

**Different types of capacitor**
Capacitors have different structures for different uses.

The original book's paper capacitor uses tin foil separated by insulating paper soaked in paraffin wax.
The foil and paper are wound into a tight roll, as Figure 155 shows.

Winding fits a large conducting area into a small space.
The picture is a structural diagram, not a claim that all modern capacitors use tin foil or paper.

Figure 156 shows an example air variable capacitor with moving and fixed groups of plates, not a radio circuit.
Such a capacitor can be used in some radio tuning circuits.**
Tuning** selects the radio signal to receive.

The capacitor has separate, insulated groups of metal plates.
Turning the knob moves a group into the gaps of the other group, changing the overlapping area of facing plates and hence the capacitance.
Facing overlap is the part of a plate directly opposite a plate in the other group.

The groups must not touch, because contact causes a **short circuit**, an unintended conducting connection across the capacitor.
Air is the **dielectric**, the insulating material between the conducting plates.
This example does not describe the method used by every modern radio device.

Figure 155

Figure 156

Figure 157

Figure 157 shows external examples of electrolytic capacitor packages, not an internal cutaway.
The following description explains their internal structure, which is not visible in that picture.

An **electrolytic capacitor** uses a very thin insulating oxide film to make the dielectric layer thin and obtain a large capacitance.
An oxide is a material formed by combining an element with oxygen.
In the structure described here, the oxide film on metal foil is the dielectric.

Paper soaked in **electrolyte**, a conducting liquid, separates the layers and holds the liquid.
The electrolyte, not the paper itself, contacts the other side of the oxide film and conducts electricity.
Do not simply treat the paper as a metal plate.

Common aluminum electrolytic capacitors have specified **polarity**, a required positive and negative connection direction, and a **rated voltage**, the specified permitted operating voltage.
Observe these limits when using them.

Consult the actual component's own marked polarity and voltage rating.
They cannot be inferred from this simplified external illustration.

Capacitors can also use other dielectrics and structures.
Choose the structure for the required capacitance, operating voltage, frequency, and application conditions.
Frequency means how often a repeating signal completes a cycle in a given time.

inventory.description: The left bus runs vertically between the upper and lower branch corners. A filled junction dot midway joins an outward left lead. The upper and lower left branch wires meet the respective positive plates. All are one conductor.

The right bus runs vertically between upper and lower branch corners. A filled junction dot midway joins an outward right lead. The upper and lower right branch wires meet the respective negative plates. This conductor is separate from the left bus.

Exactly two thick vertical separated plates on the top branch, the left positive and the right negative in the depicted charged state. C_1 is printed above the pair. +|q_1| appears above/left and -|q_1| above/right. Wires meet the middle of the respective plates. Uncalibrated clean layout replaces scan irregularities.

Exactly two thick vertical separated plates on the bottom branch, again left positive and right negative. +|q_2| is below/left, -|q_2| below/right, and C_2 below the pair. Separate q_1 and q_2 magnitudes are printed; the pixels do not assert they are equal. Uncalibrated clean layout replaces scan irregularities.
No battery, switch, current arrows, ground symbol, resistor, dielectric insert, units, numerical values, formula, caption or ellipsis is printed inside the PNG.
